name: CLEVR-MRT
ability_definition: The ability to imagine how something will look after it is moved around or when its parts are moved or rearranged.

task_realism.reasoning: The core demand is real visualization: infer what a scene looks like from a different viewpoint. The scenes, however, are synthetic CLEVR primitives (cubes, spheres, cylinders), and the questions ask about templated spatial relations and attributes. Real work that uses visualization looks quite different. Examples include picturing how an assembled part fits, how furniture or equipment would sit after repositioning, how a folded or rearranged component looks, or reading a drawing from another orientation.

evaluation_conditions.reasoning: Models are trained specifically on this task's distribution and are given the camera transformation explicitly. In real work a person usually has to infer or imagine the transformation themselves. The input distribution is narrow and procedurally generated. There is no open-world variability, clutter, occlusion from real objects, or ambiguity. There are also no tool or context demands and no stakes.

construct_coverage.reasoning: It covers only rigid whole-scene viewpoint rotation. It leaves out the other half of the construct: imagining the result when parts are moved, rearranged, folded, or assembled. It also skips multi-step transformations and non-rigid changes. Even within rotation, answers can often come from coarse relational reasoning rather than detailed mental simulation of appearance.

format_match.reasoning: Inputs are single rendered synthetic images paired with templated questions. Outputs are short categorical answers such as yes/no, counts, or attributes. Workplace visualization artifacts are sketches, CAD views, layout plans, assembly instructions, or physical manipulations, and the expected outputs are judgments or drawings rather than VQA tokens.

transferability_reasoning: CLEVR-MRT does target a genuine slice of visualization, since answering requires reasoning about a scene from a rotated viewpoint. That slice is narrow: rigid rotation only, in toy synthetic scenes, with the transform supplied and task-specific training. Its format and conditions are far from real workplace visualization, so strong performance says little about practical ability to imagine rearranged, folded, or repositioned real objects.

2022.model_or_system: The authors' self-supervised 3D contrastive volumetric encoder with a camera-conditioned FILM VQA head (Beckham et al.)
2022.human_reference: General adult workforce performing everyday spatial visualization, such as imagining a simple scene of a few objects from another viewpoint.
